items.name: Wikipedia
clues: It answers your questions, sometimes at great length, and anyone can change what it says.
Students the night before a deadline, pub-quiz cheats and people settling arguments at dinner.
Two Americans launched it in January 2001 as a side project, next to a slower online encyclopedia written only by experts.
It shows no adverts. Once a year a banner asks you, quite politely, for a small donation.
Its pages are written and checked by unpaid volunteers, who sometimes argue for weeks about what counts as a reliable source.
A Hawaiian word meaning “quick”, joined to the end of the word “encyclopedia”.

items.name: Spotify
clues: It plays whatever you want, whenever you want, and then politely suggests something similar.
More or less everyone with headphones, plus a lot of musicians who complain about how little it pays them.
Two Swedish entrepreneurs started it in Stockholm in 2006, when most young people were downloading music illegally.
You can use it free with adverts, or pay every month to make the adverts go away.
Every December, your social media fills up with people sharing their year in listening: their “Wrapped”.
One founder misheard a word the other shouted across the room. They searched for it online, found nothing, and registered it within minutes.

items.name: Duolingo
clues: It teaches you something for five minutes a day, using little games and quite a lot of guilt.
Millions of people who promise themselves they will finally learn Spanish before the summer holiday.
A professor at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh started it with his student. The professor had already helped invent CAPTCHA, the “prove you’re not a robot” test.
It’s free with adverts, or you can pay for a version with no adverts and unlimited mistakes.
In February 2025 the company announced that its mascot had died, “probably waiting for you to do your lesson”. He was brought back to life soon after.
A green owl called Duo, plus “lingo”, an informal word for a language.

items.name: Reddit
clues: Thousands and thousands of discussion forums, on everything from investing to pictures of cats that look like bread.
People asking strangers for honest advice, fans of very specific hobbies, and anyone who adds its name to the end of a search to find real opinions.
Two university roommates from Virginia started it in 2005, with money from a brand-new start-up programme in Massachusetts.
Mostly adverts, plus deals that let AI companies train their models on what users have written.
Each community is run by unpaid volunteer moderators. In June 2023 thousands of them closed their communities in protest at new company rules.
Its name sounds like what you say when you’ve finished an article: “I ___ it.” Its mascot is a little white alien.

items.name: Skyscanner
clues: You tell it where you want to go, and it searches lots of other websites for the cheapest way to get there.
Students looking for a €19 flight to Barcelona, and people who check the price eleven times before they book.
A software developer was fed up with checking every airline’s website one by one, so he wrote a program to search them all at once. It launched in 2003, and its head office is in Edinburgh.
It doesn’t sell you the ticket itself: it earns money when you click through to an airline or a travel agent.
In 2016 a Chinese travel company bought it for about £1.4 billion, one of the biggest sales of a British tech start-up at the time.
Look up: that’s the first half of the name. The second half is a machine that searches.

items.name: ChatGPT
clues: It writes your emails, explains things patiently at three in the morning, and sometimes makes facts up with total confidence.
Students, programmers, marketing teams, and your aunt, who uses it to write birthday poems.
A research lab in San Francisco released it as a free “research preview” at the end of November 2022.
It’s free to try; a monthly subscription gets you newer models and fewer limits.
It reached a million users in five days, and an estimated 100 million in about two months, faster than any app before it at the time.
The last three letters stand for “generative pre-trained transformer”. The first four are what you do with it.
